question: A planar abrupt junction has area 10⁻⁴ cm², permittivity 10⁻¹² F/cm and depletion width 10⁻⁴ cm. Find its depletion capacitance in pF.

steps: The permittivity-area product is 10⁻¹⁶ F·cm.
Divide by W=10⁻⁴ cm to obtain 10⁻¹² F.
This equals 1 pF.
commonMistakes: All length and area units must use the same centimeter convention.

hints: Identify the conditions under which junction depletion capacitance applies.
Start from $ C_j=\epsilon A/W $.

verification.method: Permittivity-area-width dimensional capacitance calculation. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: For an abrupt junction with built-in voltage Vbi=1 V, assume Cj(VR)=Cj(0)/sqrt(1+VR/Vbi). Find Cj(3 V)/Cj(0).

steps: Inside the square root the ratio is 1+3/1=4.
The square root is 2.
The capacitance ratio is 1/2, corresponding to twice the depletion width at fixed area.

hints: Identify the conditions under which reverse-bias depletion expansion applies.
Start from $ C_j(V_R)/C_j(0)=(1+V_R/V_{bi})^{-1/2} $.

question: An ideal diode has IS=1 nA, η=1 and VT=25 mV. Find the forward voltage for I=10 μA, in millivolts, retaining the −1 term in the diode law.

solution.asked: Invert the full diode current relation.
steps: Rearrange I=IS(exp(V/VT)−1) to exp(V/VT)=10001.
Multiply ln10001 by 25 mV.
The required voltage is approximately 230.261009 mV.
solution.explanation: The required voltage is approximately 230.261009 mV.
commonMistakes: The exact logarithm argument is 1+I/IS, not simply I/IS.

hints: Identify the conditions under which diode inverse exponential applies.
Start from $ V=\eta V_T\ln(1+I/I_S) $.

verification.method: Numerically invert the original diode current law with voltage measured in mV. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: In an abrupt junction depletion approximation, NA=10¹⁷ and ND=10¹⁶ cm⁻³. Find xp/xn.

given: Uniform ionized doping on each side
solution.asked: Find the ratio of p-side to n-side widths.
steps: The integrated positive and negative depletion charges must have equal magnitude.
Divide the balance by NAxn to obtain xp/xn=ND/NA.
The ratio is 10¹⁶/10¹⁷=0.1.
commonMistakes: Depletion extends farther into the more lightly doped side.

hints: Identify the conditions under which depletion charge balance applies.
Start from $ N_Ax_p=N_Dx_n $.

verification.method: Enforce equal-magnitude integrated dopant charges on both sides. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: At thermal equilibrium in an ideal PN junction, which statement is correct?

options.text: The depletion electric field must vanish
There are no mobile carriers anywhere
Electron diffusion current alone must vanish everywhere
The net terminal current is zero because transport contributions balance

steps: The built-in field and carrier gradients can both be nonzero.
Their corresponding transport contributions balance at equilibrium.
The net terminal current is zero, without requiring each individual drift or diffusion contribution to vanish. Select D.
solution.explanation: The net terminal current is zero, without requiring each individual drift or diffusion contribution to vanish. Select D.
commonMistakes: Equilibrium does not mean the absence of every microscopic transport component.

hints: Identify the conditions under which drift–diffusion balance applies.
Start from $ J_{total}=J_n+J_p=0 $.

verification.method: Equilibrium electrochemical balance with nonzero drift/diffusion components. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: Using charge-control model Q=τI with constant transit-storage time τ=10 ns, forward current I=1 mA and ideality factor 1 at VT=25 mV, use the high-forward-bias approximation dI/dV≈I/VT to find diffusion capacitance dQ/dV in pF.

solution.asked: Find τ times incremental diode conductance.
steps: The stated forward-current slope is 0.001/0.025=0.04 S.
Multiply by storage time 10⁻⁸ s to get 4×10⁻¹⁰ F.
This is 400 pF. The model concerns stored minority charge rather than depletion width.

question: A measured reverse-recovery current is a triangle with magnitude rising from zero to 2 mA and returning to zero over total duration 4 ns. Find the recovered charge magnitude in pC.

steps: The magnitude-time area is half the triangle’s base times height.
The recovered charge magnitude is 4 pC.

question: Which statements about an ideal abrupt reverse-biased PN junction before breakdown are correct?

options.text: Depletion width generally increases with reverse bias
The depletion region becomes perfectly conducting
Junction capacitance generally decreases as depletion widens
Space charge arises primarily from uncovered ionized dopants in the depletion approximation

steps: Greater reverse potential requires a wider space-charge region in this model.
Its small-signal capacitance decreases because separation W increases.
The depleted mobile carriers leave fixed dopant ions; this is not a perfectly conducting region. Select A, C and D.
solution.explanation: The depleted mobile carriers leave fixed dopant ions; this is not a perfectly conducting region. Select A, C and D.
commonMistakes: Depleted carrier density does not imply zero electric field.

hints: Identify the conditions under which reverse-bias depletion electrostatics applies.
Start from $ W\propto\sqrt{V_{bi}+V_R},\quad C_j=\epsilon A/W $.

verification.method: Abrupt-junction Poisson depletion scaling and fixed-charge versus mobile-conduction distinction. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: A junction has total depletion width W=1.1 μm and NA/ND=10. Find the n-side depletion width xn in μm.

solution.asked: Find the more lightly doped side’s width.
steps: Charge balance gives xp=xn/10.
Substitute into total width: 1.1=1.1xn in μm.
Thus xn=1 μm and xp=0.1 μm.
solution.explanation: Thus xn=1 μm and xp=0.1 μm.
commonMistakes: Do not split the width equally for unequal dopings.

hints: Identify the conditions under which combined depletion width constraints applies.
Start from $ x_p=x_n/10,\quad W=x_p+x_n $.

verification.method: Simultaneous total-width and dopant-charge constraints. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: At equilibrium in a semiconductor PN junction at uniform temperature, which statements hold?

options.text: The Fermi level is spatially constant
Built-in electric field can be nonzero
The net external short-circuit current is a sustained power source
The built-in field and diffusion effects can balance

steps: A constant equilibrium Fermi level reflects no net electrochemical driving force.
Band bending and an internal field can coexist with this equilibrium because diffusion balances drift.
Such a junction cannot deliver sustained external power at equilibrium. Select A, B and D.
solution.explanation: Such a junction cannot deliver sustained external power at equilibrium. Select A, B and D.
commonMistakes: An internal electrostatic barrier is not evidence of a perpetual DC source.

hints: Identify the conditions under which electrochemical equilibrium applies.
Start from $ \nabla E_F=0\quad\text{at thermal equilibrium} $.

verification.method: Uniform equilibrium Fermi-level condition and drift/diffusion cancellation; no external power source. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.
